topics.title: Sources of Law, Intentional Torts & Privacy
topics.summary: Nursing law comes from four sources. Intentional torts like assault, battery, and false imprisonment are prevented by getting consent, using the least restraint, and guarding health information.
objectives: You can name the four sources of law and give a nursing example of each.
You can explain how the Nurse Practice Act and Board of Nursing work together.
You can tell criminal law from civil law.
You can label a scene as assault, battery, false imprisonment, defamation, or invasion of privacy.
You can apply HIPAA to calls, visitors, charts, and social media.
You can respond safely when a competent client refuses care or wants to leave.
topics.bigPicture:
Almost every nursing action has a legal side. Your license comes from a state law. A state agency, the Board of Nursing, writes the rules for what you may do. Each time you touch a client, close a door, chart a note, or answer a phone call, the law is in the room.

You do not need to become a lawyer. You need to spot when a normal action crosses a line. The NCLEX tests this with real moments: a nurse who threatens a shot, a client tied down without an order, a nurse peeking at a neighbor’s chart. The safe answer respects the client’s choice, gets consent, uses the least restraint, and shares only what is needed.
recap: Law comes from the Constitution, statutes, administrative rules, and common law.
The NPA is a statute. The Board of Nursing enforces it.
Criminal law: the state prosecutes. Civil law: a person sues for money.
Intentional torts are willful acts. Intent to act counts, not intent to harm.
Assault is the threat. Battery is the touch. False imprisonment is holding without legal right.
A competent adult may refuse care or leave AMA. Explore why, notify, explain, document.
Share health information only on a need-to-know, minimum-necessary basis.

keyTerms.def: The full set of rules a society lives by (Guido, 2020). Made at federal, state, and local levels.
Law from the U.S. Constitution. It lets states protect health and safety. Examples: due process, equal protection.
Laws passed by a legislature. The Nurse Practice Act is a state statute.
Rules written by an agency a legislature has empowered. Board of Nursing rules are administrative law.
Law made by judges. Later courts follow earlier rulings, called precedent.
The state law that defines nursing, sets license rules and scope of practice, creates the Board, and lists reasons for discipline.
What a nurse at a given license level may legally do, set by the NPA and Board rules.
Public law about acts that harm a person or society. The government prosecutes. Punishment is a fine or prison.
Felonies are serious crimes, like homicide or major theft. Misdemeanors are lesser crimes.
Private law between people. The injured person sues, usually for money. Includes contracts and torts.
Civil law about agreements: nurse and employer, nurse and client, nurse and insurer, client and agency.
A civil wrong against a person or property. It can be intentional, or unintentional (negligence).
A wrong the person meant to do. Intent to act, not intent to harm, is what counts.
Making someone reasonably fear an unwanted touch. No touch is needed.
Touching a person, their clothes, or what they hold without consent.
Holding or confining a person without legal right, such as restraints with no order or blocking a competent client from leaving.
A false statement shared with others that harms a reputation. Libel is written. Slander is spoken.
Sharing private information or intruding on a person’s space without permission, including name, photos, belongings, and room.
PHI is protected health information: conditions, care, payment, and identifiers like name or birth date. HIPAA’s Privacy Rule protects it.
Use or share only the smallest amount of health information the task needs.
Leaving before the provider says it is safe. A competent adult has this right.

sections.heading: Where does nursing law come from?
sections.keyIdea: Law comes in layers: the Constitution, statutes like the Nurse Practice Act, Board rules, and court decisions.
sections.body:
Think of law as layers. The Constitution is on top. It protects rights like due process and lets states protect health and safety. Licensing nurses is one way states do that.

Next come statutes, passed by legislatures. Every state has a Nurse Practice Act (NPA). Legislatures can’t write every detail, so they let agencies write rules. Those rules are administrative law. The Board of Nursing is the agency that interprets and enforces the NPA.

Last is common law, made by judges. Much of tort law grew this way.

The NPA and Board rules set your scope of practice. A job description or policy can narrow it, never widen it. Policies exist to keep clients safe and to protect staff and the agency. Clients have a legal right to expect competent nursing care.

table.caption: Sources of law (Figure 49.1)
rows: Due process before a license is taken; equal protection
NPA, statutes of limitation, abuse-reporting laws, Good Samaritan acts, advance directive and informed consent laws, ADA
Agencies a statute empowers (Board of Nursing, DEA)
Board rules on scope, delegation, licensing, and discipline
Rulings on what a reasonably prudent nurse would do

sections.analogy: Think of a board game. The Constitution is the box. The NPA is the rulebook. Board rules are the referee’s FAQ. Common law is the list of past referee calls.

check.q: A hospital job description lists a task that Board rules don’t allow an LPN to do. Which rule controls?
check.a: The NPA and Board rules. An employer can narrow scope but never widen it. The LPN should decline and tell the supervisor.

sections.heading: Criminal law vs. civil law
sections.keyIdea: Criminal law punishes wrongs against society. Civil law lets an injured person sue. One act can bring both, plus Board discipline.
sections.body:
Criminal law is public law. The government brings the case, and punishment is a fine or prison. Crimes involving nurses include drug diversion, active euthanasia, sexual assault of a client, and theft.

Civil law is private law. The injured person, the plaintiff, sues the defendant for money, called damages. Contracts and torts are civil law.

Each system has its own rules. A nurse who steals a client’s oxycodone can face criminal charges, a civil suit, and Board action. A “not guilty” verdict does not protect the license.

table.caption: Table 49.1 — Categories of law (examples)
rows: Homicide, manslaughter, theft, arson, active euthanasia, sexual assault, illegal possession of controlled drugs
Nurse and employer; nurse and client; nurse and insurer; client and agency
Negligence, libel and slander, invasion of privacy, assault and battery, false imprisonment, abandonment

sections.example: A spouse says, “He’s suffering. Give him enough morphine to end this tonight.” Active euthanasia is a crime, whatever the family wants. The nurse says, “I can’t give medicine to end his life. Tell me what has been hardest to watch.” Then the nurse seeks better comfort care and palliative care. Threatening to call police is not therapeutic.

sections.heading: What makes a tort “intentional”?
sections.keyIdea: If the nurse meant to do the act without consent, it is an intentional tort, even with a good motive and no harm.
sections.body:
Negligence is unintentional, like forgetting a bed alarm. An intentional tort is an act the nurse meant to do. A good motive does not cancel it.

Assault is a threat that makes the client fear an unwanted touch. No contact is needed. “Hold still or I’ll strap you down” can be assault.

Battery is the unwanted touch itself. Examples: an injection the client refused, a catheter after a “no,” forcing a client to walk, or going on after consent is withdrawn. It is battery even if the care helps.
steps: Explain what you will do and get consent. Holding out an arm is implied consent for routine care. Procedures need informed consent.
If the client refuses, stop. Ask why and give information.
Notify the provider and document the refusal and teaching.
Never threaten or force.
sections.example: A client refuses enoxaparin because the bruises hurt. The nurse says, “I’ll tell your doctor you’re being difficult.” That is coercion. Better: explain that it prevents clots, offer to rotate sites, and respect a final “no.” Notify the provider and document.

check.q: A nurse holds a competent client’s arm as she pulls away and gives an IM antiemetic “to help her.” Which tort?
check.a: Battery. The nurse meant to touch her without consent. Intent to act defines it, not intent to harm.

sections.heading: What is false imprisonment?
sections.keyIdea: Holding a person without legal right is false imprisonment. A competent adult may leave against medical advice.
sections.body:
False imprisonment is holding a person without legal right. Examples: restraints with no order or reason, or blocking a competent client from leaving AMA. Hiding clothes or threatening security counts too.

Restraints are legal only with an order (or emergency use per policy, then a prompt order), after less restrictive steps fail, when the client is at immediate risk of harming self or others. They are time-limited and closely monitored. Never use them for convenience or punishment. A court order or legal psychiatric hold is not false imprisonment.

When a competent client wants to leave AMA:
steps: Ask calmly why the client wants to leave. The problem can often be fixed.
Check capacity. Confusion, intoxication, or psychosis changes things; follow policy.
Notify the provider.
Explain risks and offer the AMA form. The client may refuse to sign.
Never block exits, take belongings, or threaten.
If the client leaves, remove the IV safely and give discharge instructions.
Document the talk, risks explained, the client’s words, and the time.

check.q: A confused client keeps climbing out of bed. A nurse wants a vest restraint “until shift change.” What should happen?
check.a: No order and no alternatives tried risks false imprisonment. Find the cause. Try toileting, a bed alarm, a low bed, rounding, or a sitter. Call the provider if restraint seems needed.

sections.heading: Defamation and invasion of privacy
sections.keyIdea: Chart facts, not labels. Privacy covers a client’s information and also their space and belongings.
sections.body:
Defamation is a false statement, shared with others, that harms a reputation. Libel is written, including charts, emails, and posts. Slander is spoken. Charting “drug seeker” may be libel. Chart facts instead: “Requested hydromorphone at 1300 and 1400. States pain 8/10.” Concerns about a coworker’s impairment go through proper reporting, not gossip.

Privacy covers information and territory. Don’t share a client’s name, photos, or video without permission. Clients control their belongings and room. Search only for a clear safety reason, per policy, with a witness and documentation.
sections.example: A student photographs a client’s unusual tattoo, cropping out the face. The tattoo can still identify the client. She should delete it, tell the instructor, and follow agency policy.

sections.heading: HIPAA: who may know what?
sections.keyIdea: See or share health information only when your job needs it, only the minimum needed, and only with permission or legal authority.
sections.body:
HIPAA protects PHI, any health or payment information that could identify a client. It is the federal minimum. A stricter state law or policy wins.

One leak can bring a privacy lawsuit, HIPAA fines or criminal penalties, and Board discipline. Leaving out a name is not enough: time, age, and injury can identify a client. If a coworker posts client details, report it to your manager. Don’t reply publicly.
bullets: Need to know: only the care team looks, for treatment, payment, or operations. Looking up a neighbor or relative is a breach.
The client decides who else knows. Verify callers with a passcode.
Legal exceptions: suspected abuse and reportable diseases must be reported.
Lock screens, never share passwords, and never discuss clients in public or online.

table.caption: Applying HIPAA
rows: Reading a coworker’s chart out of curiosity
Telling a caller who says he is the brother about the diagnosis
Not until identity and the client’s permission are verified
Telling an employer a client has HIV

check.q: A nurse opens her neighbor’s chart “to make sure he’s okay” and tells no one. Is this a violation?
check.a: Yes. Opening PHI with no work need is a breach. Access logs show who looked.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Look-alike terms cause most wrong answers. The verb in the stem usually tells you which one it is.
sections.body: Find the one clue that separates each pair.

rows: Threat (“if you don’t…”) vs. touch (“gives,” “holds down”).
Meant to do the act? Intentional tort. An unintended slip is negligence.
Lawful restraint has an order, a reason, and monitoring.
Reporting abuse or reportable disease is required, not a breach.
The legislature writes the NPA. The Board writes rules.
State prosecutes (“felony”) vs. a person sues (“damages”).

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect to name the tort, or to pick the response that respects a competent client’s choice without threats or force.
sections.body:
Common patterns: name the tort, choose the best response to a refusal or AMA request, or spot the privacy statement that needs more teaching.

Sample: An alert, oriented client on a heparin drip says, “I’m going home now,” and starts to dress. What should the nurse do first?
A. Say security will be called.
B. Ask what is prompting the decision to leave.
C. Remove the IV so the client can leave safely.
D. Have the client sign the AMA form.
steps: Read the stem: a competent adult wants to leave; the word is “first.”
What is it really asking? The first step in an AMA situation.
Key cues: “alert and oriented” means the right to leave. The heparin drip makes leaving risky.
A is wrong: threats are coercion and can be false imprisonment.
C and D are wrong: they come later, after the reason is explored and the provider knows.
The answer is B. Asking why may solve the problem and respects autonomy.
Strategy: explore the reason first. Any option that threatens or forces is wrong.

sections.heading: Worked case: the refused catheter
sections.keyIdea: A competent client’s “no” ends the procedure, and visitors get no details without the client’s permission.
sections.body: Mrs. Alvarez, 72, is alert and has urinary retention after surgery. She refuses an ordered straight catheter. An assistant says, “I’ll hold her legs.” Later, a man says he is her son and asks if it was cancer.
steps: Cues: a competent refusal, a coworker offering force, and an unverified visitor.
Analyze: going ahead is battery; holding her is an unjustified restraint.
Act: stop, ask why, and offer privacy, positioning, and a bladder scan.
Tell the provider about the refusal and scan result.
Teach the assistant privately that forcing care is battery.
Visitor: share nothing unless she agrees.
Document her words, teaching, alternatives, and provider notice.

check.q: She agrees, then midway says, “Stop, it hurts.” What now?
check.a: Stop. Consent can be withdrawn anytime. Assess her pain and tell the provider.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: In NC, the Nursing Practice Act is the statute, and NCBON rules are the administrative law.
sections.body: The NCLEX won’t ask statute numbers. Know these for practice.
bullets: The NC Board of Nursing (NCBON) regulates nursing under the NC Nursing Practice Act (G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.).
RN practice rules are in 21 NCAC 36 .0224; LPN rules are in .0225.
The RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment. The LPN works under supervision.
The NCBON publishes scope-of-practice and delegation decision trees.
NC is a Nurse Licensure Compact state. Follow the practice laws of the state where the client is.
Diversion, impairment, fraud, misconduct, and confidentiality breaches are reported to the NCBON.
NC is a universal reporting state: anyone suspecting child maltreatment reports to the county DSS (G.S. 7B-301). Disabled adults are reported to DSS too (G.S. 108A-102).
These mandatory reports are legal exceptions to confidentiality, never privacy violations.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body: Source: Module 49 study guide, pp. 2825–2829.
bullets: Pp. 2825–2827: sources of law, Figure 49.1, Table 49.1. Pp. 2828–2829: intentional torts, privacy, HIPAA.
The course links privacy to the Fourth Amendment, which limits government searches. In health care, HIPAA, state law, and the privacy tort protect privacy.
Restraint rules, AMA steps, and HIPAA’s “minimum necessary” are standard national practice, added for application.

mnemonics.name: Threat vs. Touch
mnemonics.text: Assault = Apprehension (a threat; no touch needed). Battery = Body contact without consent. If the nurse only said it, think assault. If the nurse did it, think battery.

mnemonics.name: Libel = Lasting, Slander = Spoken
mnemonics.text: Libel leaves a lasting written record (chart, email, post). Slander is spoken and fades into the air.

pearls: A good motive never cures battery.
Never block the door for a competent adult leaving AMA.
Opening a chart with no work reason is a breach, even if you tell no one.
Mandatory reports are legal exceptions to confidentiality.
redFlags: A plan to hold or tie a competent client “for their own good.”
Restraints for convenience or without an order.
Client photos or posts, even without names.
Threats like “If you don’t…, I’ll…” to get cooperation.
Phone or visitor requests for client details from someone not verified or authorized.

checks.q: A nurse says, “If you won’t swallow it, I’ll give it as a shot.” The client swallows it. Did a tort occur?
checks.a: Possibly assault. The threat created fear of an unwanted touch, even with no touch. Instead, explore the refusal, teach, and notify the provider.

checks.q: An alert client with chest pain says he is leaving to pick up his child. What should the nurse do, in order?
checks.a: Explore the reason and look for solutions, like someone else getting the child. Assess capacity. Notify the provider. Explain risks and offer the AMA form. Remove devices safely if he goes. Document.

checks.q: A Board revokes a license after a criminal “not guilty” verdict. How?
checks.a: Licensure is administrative law, separate from criminal law, with its own standards.

checks.q: A husband asks for his wife’s pregnancy result. She asked you not to tell him. What do you say?
checks.a: You can’t share health information without her permission; he can ask her.

checks.q: A nurse charts, “Daughter is stealing pain pills.” What is better?
checks.a: Chart facts: pill counts, times, who was present. Report the concern properly. The label may be libel.

checks.q: A Board of Nursing rule says which tasks may be delegated to assistive personnel. Which source of law is it?
checks.a: Administrative law. It is an agency rule that carries out the statute, the Nurse Practice Act.

topics.title: Negligence, Malpractice & the Standard of Care
topics.summary: Malpractice is professional negligence that harms a client. Nurses prevent it by meeting the standard of care, speaking up, supervising, reporting errors, and documenting well.
objectives: You can tell negligence from malpractice and name the standard a student meets.
You can apply the six elements of malpractice to a case.
You can sort a mistake into a Box 49.1 category.
You can explain respondeat superior, res ipsa loquitur, and the statute of limitations.
You can respond to an error in order and classify it with Just Culture.
You can write defensive documentation and compare insurance types.
topics.bigPicture:
Most lawsuits against nurses come from ordinary misses. A fall-risk client was left with the bed high. A high potassium was never called in. In 2018, nurses were responsible for 795 of 11,810 malpractice payments in the National Practitioner Data Bank, just under 7%.

The legal test for malpractice makes a great bedside checklist. Did I have a duty? Did I do what a careful nurse would do? Could I foresee harm? Did my action cause it? On the NCLEX, the safest answer puts the client first, follows the standard, tells the provider, and reports honestly.
recap: Negligence falls below what a reasonable person would do. Malpractice is negligence by a professional, judged against a reasonably prudent nurse.
Nursing students are held to the licensed RN standard. If unsure, stop and ask.
Malpractice needs all six elements: duty, breach, foreseeability, causation, injury or harm, and damages.
Box 49.1: failure to follow standards, to communicate and document, to advocate, and to supervise.
The NPA and Board rules are the main legal basis of the standard of care.
After an error, assess the client first. Then notify, document facts, and file an incident report.
Never mention the incident report in the chart.
Occurrence policies cover any incident during the policy, whenever the claim comes. Claims-made needs both incident and claim during the policy.

keyTerms.def: Falling below what a reasonable person would do, causing unintended harm.
Professional negligence: falling below the standard of a reasonably skilled member of the profession while doing professional work.
Being legally responsible. The plaintiff must prove every element.
A legal obligation to meet a standard of care. It starts when the nurse accepts the client’s care.
Falling below the standard. Commission is doing wrong; omission is failing to act.
A careful nurse should have expected harm to follow.
The breach directly caused the injury.
Physical, financial, or emotional harm from the breach.
Money for harm: medical costs, lost wages, pain and suffering, and punitive damages if conduct was malicious or wanton.
What a reasonably prudent nurse with similar education and experience would do in similar circumstances.
“Let the master answer.” The employer is liable for employees’ acts on the job.
“The thing speaks for itself.” The harm shows negligence even though no specific person can be pinned.
The deadline to sue, counted from when the client knew or should have known of the injury.
Judging the behavior behind an error, not just the outcome: human error, at-risk, or reckless.
Insurance covering incidents during the policy, whenever the claim is filed.
Insurance covering an incident only if the incident and claim both happen during the policy, unless “tail” coverage is bought.
Timely, factual, complete charting that shows assessments, actions, responses, and provider notification.

sections.heading: Negligence vs. malpractice: whose standard?
sections.keyIdea: Malpractice is negligence by a professional, judged against a reasonably prudent nurse. Students meet the RN standard.
sections.body:
Negligence is falling below what a reasonable person would do and causing harm you didn’t intend. Malpractice is negligence by a professional at work. The yardstick becomes a reasonably prudent nurse with similar training. A critical care nurse is judged against careful critical care nurses.

Nursing students are held to the licensed RN standard. “I’m just a student” is never a defense. If unsure, stop and get help first.

A breach can be commission, like the wrong dose. It can be omission, like not reporting a change.

rows: A wet floor at home trips a guest
A fall-risk client’s bed is left high; the client breaks a hip

check.q: A student is told to hang a blood transfusion she has never given. Her instructor is across the unit. What should she do?
check.a: Wait and get her instructor first. Acting without competence would be a breach of the RN standard.

sections.heading: Where does the standard of care come from?
sections.keyIdea: The NPA and Board rules are the main source. Job descriptions, policies, and national standards add detail.
sections.body:
The main legal basis is the Nurse Practice Act and Board rules. They change, so stay current. In court, expert witnesses explain what the standard required.

Safety ties in. As many as 1 in 10 hospitalized clients have an adverse event, many involving drugs. Reporting errors reveals root causes. Covering them up brings serious consequences. Managers must make sure tasks are delegated correctly.
bullets: NPA and Board rules: the primary legal basis.
Job description: can limit scope, never expand it past the NPA.
Agency policies: follow them. If one conflicts with evidence, fix it through quality improvement.
National standards: ANA and specialty standards.

table.caption: Legal issues and related concepts
rows: Teach at the client’s level, help assess capacity, and work with a surrogate if capacity is lacking.
Support the legal right to end-of-life care. Medicare and Medicaid hospitals must give advance directive information.
Protect privacy, follow HIPAA, and discuss care only with the right people.

sections.example: A unit policy still calls for routine saline flushes before suctioning, which current evidence doesn’t support. The nurse doesn’t just ignore the policy. She brings the evidence to the practice council or manager so it gets updated.

sections.heading: Box 49.1: four ways nurses are negligent
sections.keyIdea: Most malpractice fits four buckets: not following standards, not communicating, not advocating, and not supervising.
sections.body:
Know every drug before you give it: why it is ordered, the dose range, side effects, toxic levels, and contraindications. “The provider ordered it” never defends a clearly unsafe dose. Hold it and clarify. Never change the dose yourself.

If a provider won’t answer a critical value, charting and waiting is a failure to act. Keep watching the client and go up the chain of command: charge nurse, supervisor, then medical director or rapid response. Document each try.
bullets: Failure to follow standards: incomplete assessment, ignoring policy or orders, unsafe environment, not monitoring.
Failure to communicate and document: not reporting findings, labs, or changes to the provider and team.
Failure to advocate: not questioning unsafe, incomplete, or unreadable orders; not reporting unsafe practice.
Failure to supervise: not knowing or checking the skills of people you supervise.

check.q: At 0310 a potassium is 6.4 mEq/L with peaked T waves. Two pages go unanswered. What next?
check.a: Keep monitoring and escalate up the chain of command per policy, such as the charge nurse or rapid response. Document each attempt.

table.caption: Box 49.1 applied
rows: Gives metoprolol with an apical pulse of 46
Charts a potassium of 6.2 but never calls
Gives 10 times the usual dose “as ordered”
Never checks a new aide’s vital signs on a post-op client
Knows the aide’s skills and follows up

sections.heading: What must be proven? The six elements
sections.keyIdea: Malpractice needs all six elements. If one is missing, such as harm, there is no malpractice.
sections.body:
If one element is missing, the claim fails. A favorite trap: a wrong drug with no harm. That is a breach without malpractice. It still must be reported.

Three legal ideas often come up in these cases:

table.caption: Six elements (p. 2828)
rows: Did the nurse owe this client care?
Did the nurse fall below the standard?
Should a careful nurse have expected harm?
Did the breach directly cause the injury?
Was there physical, financial, or emotional harm?
What money makes up for it?

bullets: Respondeat superior: the hospital answers for employees and is usually named too. It is also liable for poor staffing, training, or orientation. The nurse stays personally accountable.
Res ipsa loquitur: the harm itself shows negligence, like a retained sponge or a burn under anesthesia.
Statute of limitations: the deadline to sue. The course gives 1 to 2 years as typical; it varies by state and is longer for minors.
sections.analogy: Picture a chain of six links. Break any link and the case falls. Look for the missing link.

check.q: A nurse gives a double dose of acetaminophen. The client is fine. Which element is missing?
check.a: Injury or harm. Still assess, notify the provider, and report the error.

sections.heading: Preventing errors and responding to them
sections.keyIdea: Prevent errors with safety systems. When one happens, assess the client first, then report honestly.
sections.body:
Medication errors are a leading cause of claims. Use clear orders, barcode scanning, double checks, and two identifiers. Take every complaint seriously; a sudden severe headache could be a brain bleed. Falls are a common cause of lawsuits, so assess fall risk and document every precaution.

Just Culture judges the behavior, not the outcome. A risky shortcut is at-risk even if no one is hurt yet.

When an error happens, follow these steps in order:
steps: Assess the client first.
Act to limit harm and notify the provider.
Chart objective facts, with no blame and no mention of the incident report.
File an incident report. It is a quality tool, not part of the chart.
Disclose to the client per policy.

table.caption: Just Culture
rows: At-risk (a shortcut whose risk seems small)

check.q: A nurse gave insulin to the wrong client. What is first?
check.a: Assess that client’s glucose and alertness and treat low blood sugar. Then notify, chart facts, and file a report.

sections.heading: Documentation and liability insurance
sections.keyIdea: If it wasn’t charted, a jury may assume it wasn’t done. Know which insurance covers you, and when.
sections.body:
Clients who feel heard and informed sue less. The chart is the legal record. Chart promptly and objectively. Show assessments, actions, the client’s response, and provider notice. Quote the client when it helps.

Never chart ahead or rely on memory. Never alter or delete an entry; use the EHR correction process. Chart only your own care. When you call a provider, record who, when, what you reported, and what was ordered. Students usually must carry liability insurance.

table.caption: Liability insurance compared
rows: Any incident during the policy, whenever the claim comes
Only if incident and claim both happen during the policy; needs “tail” after
Broadest: any setting within scope, including off-duty help
Only acts done as an employee at work

sections.example: Poor: “Client doing fine. Doctor aware.” Better: “1420 BP 84/50, HR 118, dizzy. 1425 Dr. Kim notified; bolus ordered. 1515 BP 104/66.”

check.q: A nurse says, “Respondeat superior means I don’t need my own insurance.” True?
check.a: No. She can be named personally, and employer coverage only covers work acts.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: A breach alone is not malpractice, and the incident report never goes in the chart.
sections.body: Look for the clue word in the stem.

rows: Malpractice is negligence by a professional, judged by the professional standard.
Predictable harm vs. harm actually caused.
Employer liability vs. the harm proves negligence.
Claims-made needs the claim during the policy.
Never chart that a report was filed.
Policy can limit scope, never expand it (“the unit allows aides to…”).

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: When an order doesn’t fit the client’s condition, hold, clarify, and notify.
sections.body:
Sample: Digoxin 0.25 mg is due. Apical pulse is 52 and potassium is 3.1 mEq/L. Best action?
A. Give it and document the pulse.
B. Hold it and notify the provider.
C. Give half the dose.
D. Hold it and document only.
steps: Read the stem: an order exists, but the client’s data make it unsafe right now.
What is it really asking? The action that meets the standard of care and the advocate role.
Key cues: a pulse under 60 and low potassium raise the risk of digoxin toxicity. Harm is foreseeable.
Why A is wrong: giving an unsafe dose fails to advocate. Charting doesn’t fix it.
Why C is wrong: a nurse can’t change a prescribed dose.
Why D is wrong: holding is right, but not telling the provider fails to communicate.
The answer is B. Then document the hold, the call, and the reply.
Strategy: when an order conflicts with the client’s condition, hold, clarify, and notify.
bullets: Which element is missing? Usually harm or causation.
After an error, what first? Assess the client.
Best chart entry: objective, timed, with provider notice.
Advocacy: questioning an order that doesn’t fit the client.

sections.heading: Worked case: the fall at 0300
sections.keyIdea: When a high-risk client falls, care for the client first, then notify, chart facts, and report.
sections.body:
Mr. Thompson, 81, has pneumonia and a high fall-risk score. He takes a sleeping pill and furosemide. At 0300 he is on the floor. The bed is high, the alarm is off, and the call light is out of reach. His right hip hurts, and the leg looks short and turned out.

The assistant says, “I turned off the alarm because it kept going off.”
steps: Cues: high risk, a sedative and a diuretic, missing precautions, and signs of hip fracture.
Analyze: duty, breach, foreseeability, causation, and harm may all be present.
Client first: don’t move him until assessed. Check airway, alertness, vital signs, and neuro status. Get help and use lift equipment.
Notify the provider using SBAR. Expect imaging and pain orders. Notify family per policy.
Chart facts: time found, his words, findings, and the room as found. No blame, and no mention of the incident report.
File an incident report so the alarm problem gets reviewed.
Coach the assistant on why the alarm matters. The RN is accountable for supervising delegated care.

check.q: Which earlier charting would best defend the nurse?
check.a: A fall-risk assessment and the precautions put in place and checked.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: In NC, the NPA and NCBON rules set the standard, and lawsuit deadlines are longer than the course range.
sections.body: These apply to NC practice. The NCLEX tests national principles.
bullets: The NC Nursing Practice Act (G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.) and NCBON rules, 21 NCAC 36 .0224 (RN) and .0225 (LPN), are the main basis of the standard.
The RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment. The LPN works under RN or provider supervision.
The RN may delegate tasks, but not the nursing process or nursing judgment.
Nurse Aide I: registry kept by NC DHHS Division of Health Service Regulation.
Nurse Aide II: registry kept by the NCBON; must also be on the NA I registry. Some advanced tasks, like sterile dressing changes and oxygen, per the NCBON list.
A task must be on the aide’s list, and the RN must decide it fits that client. Use the NCBON “Decision Tree for Delegation to UAP.”
NCBON Just Culture–based Complaint Evaluation Tool: human error (console), at-risk behavior (coach), reckless behavior (discipline).
Diversion, impairment, fraud, misconduct, and confidentiality breaches go to the NCBON, not only the employer. The NCBON offers alternative-to-discipline programs for substance use.
Malpractice statute of limitations: generally 3 years, with a 4-year statute of repose (G.S. 1-15(c)).
NC keeps pure contributory negligence as a defense. A plaintiff who helped cause their own injury may be barred from recovery.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body: Source: Module 49 study guide, pp. 2825–2831.
bullets: Pp. 2825–2828: malpractice data, Box 49.1, six elements, medication safety alert, respondeat superior, res ipsa loquitur, statute of limitations.
Pp. 2829–2831: related concepts, prevention, falls safety alert, liability insurance, standard of care.
Many texts list four elements (duty, breach, causation, damages). This course lists six. Learn the six.
The course’s 1 to 2 years is state-specific. NC is generally 3 years, with a 4-year repose.
Assess-first error steps, keeping the incident report out of the chart, SBAR, two identifiers, and tail coverage are standard practice, added for application.

NC delegation and NCBON Just Culture content came from verified NCBON information. National Just Culture categories and chain-of-command escalation are standard safety practice, not in the course text.

mnemonics.name: Doctors Bring Four Coffees In Dallas
mnemonics.text: The six elements in order: Duty, Breach, Foreseeability, Causation, Injury or harm, Damages. Missing any one breaks the case.

mnemonics.name: Occurrence = “Once covered, always covered”
mnemonics.text: If it happened during the policy, you are covered whenever the claim arrives. Claims-made: both the event and the claim must fall inside the policy window.

pearls: Wrong drug, no harm means a breach without malpractice. Still assess, notify, document, and report.
After an error, assess the client first. Paperwork comes after safety.
Never write “incident report completed” in the chart.
Hold and clarify an order that conflicts with the client’s condition. Notify the provider. Never change the dose yourself.
Respondeat superior adds the employer to the suit. It does not remove the nurse’s own accountability.
Document the fall-risk assessment and every precaution. That record is your defense.
redFlags: A critical lab or change in condition that is charted but not reported to the provider.
An order that is unreadable, incomplete, or outside the usual dose range for the client.
A delegated task whose results the RN never checks, especially for an unstable client.
Alarms off, bed high, or call light out of reach for a high-fall-risk client.
Pressure from anyone to change, delay, or leave out documentation of an error.

checks.q: A nurse has an aide walk a client 2 hours after hip surgery without checking orthostatic vital signs. The client faints and breaks a wrist. Which Box 49.1 category applies, and which elements are present?
checks.a: Failure to supervise, and to follow standards. Duty, breach, foreseeability (post-op dizziness risk), causation, injury, and damages are all likely present.

checks.q: Three years after surgery, a client learns a sponge was left in her abdomen. Which legal ideas may apply?
checks.a: Res ipsa loquitur (the harm shows negligence without naming who), respondeat superior (the hospital answers for employees), and the statute of limitations, counted from when she knew or should have known.

checks.q: A nurse drops a claims-made policy when she changes jobs. Two years later she is sued for care given under that policy. Is she covered?
checks.a: No, unless she bought tail coverage. Claims-made needs the claim while the policy is active. An occurrence policy would have covered it.

checks.q: A client’s glucose is 42 mg/dL. The nurse treats it and rechecks but never charts it. Why is this a legal problem?
checks.a: The chart is the legal record. With no entry, there is no proof the care happened. Failure to document is its own Box 49.1 category.

checks.q: Which entry is better: “Client upset and uncooperative,” or “Client stated, ‘I’m not taking that pill,’ and turned away; purpose explained; provider notified at 1015”?
checks.a: The second. It is objective, quotes the client, and shows teaching and provider notice with a time.

checks.q: Nurse 1 grabs a look-alike heparin vial from a cluttered drawer. Nurse 2 skips barcode scans because “it slows me down.” Nurse 3 works impaired. Classify each using Just Culture.
checks.a: Nurse 1: human error; console and fix the system. Nurse 2: at-risk behavior; coach and fix the slow scanner. Nurse 3: reckless behavior; discipline and report to the Board as required.

topics.title: Consent, Competency & Laws Across the Lifespan
topics.summary: The provider gets informed consent; the nurse checks understanding and witnesses. Laws on capacity, minors, controlled drugs, Good Samaritan care, whistleblowing, and abuse reporting guide care across the lifespan.
objectives: You can list the five elements of informed consent and who does what.
You can tell expressed, implied, and emergency consent apart.
You can name the right decision maker: client, guardian, surrogate, parent, or minor.
You can handle controlled drugs safely and spot diversion.
You can state when Good Samaritan and whistleblower laws protect a nurse.
You can report suspected abuse and explain the limits of teen privacy.
topics.bigPicture:
Consent is the line between care and battery. Checking that a form is signed is only part of the job. The nurse makes sure the client can see, hear, read, and understand. The nurse brings in a medical interpreter and makes sure no one is pressuring the client. When the client can’t decide, the nurse must know who can.

This lesson also covers laws that protect children and vulnerable adults, control risky drugs, and protect nurses who do the right thing. Each has a condition the NCLEX loves. Emergency consent doesn’t override a prior refusal. Good Samaritan protection ends if you abandon the victim. Abuse reports need suspicion, not proof.
recap: Informed consent needs capacity, five elements (reason, procedure, benefits, risks, alternatives), and a free choice.
The provider gets consent. The nurse checks understanding, gets an interpreter, and witnesses.
Emergency consent is presumed, except for a treatment the client already refused.
Competency is legal (a court). Capacity is clinical and decision-specific.
Minors need a parent unless emancipated, an emergency, a court order, mature-minor law, or a law allows that service.
Controlled drugs: secure, count, waste with a watching witness, and report gaps now.
Good Samaritan: unpaid, off-duty, within training, no abandonment. Whistleblowers report inside first.
Report suspected child or vulnerable-adult abuse in good faith, without proof.

keyTerms.def: The client’s right to be told about a treatment and to accept or refuse it, freely and without pressure.
Agreement that is spoken or written.
Agreement shown by actions, like holding out an arm. Also presumed in true emergencies.
Consent is presumed when life or limb is at risk and the client can’t consent. It never allows a treatment refused before.
A legal status. Adults (usually 18+) are presumed competent unless a court rules otherwise.
A clinical, decision-specific judgment that a person can understand, reason, and state a choice. It can change.
A person a court appoints for a legally incompetent adult. Must give the team a copy of the court order.
Short-term loss of decision ability from opioids or illness, or gradual loss from dementia.
A person authorized by law, directive, or policy to decide when the client lacks capacity.
A living will states treatment wishes. A health care power of attorney names an agent to decide.
A minor living free of parents’ control and managing their own money, or emancipated by state law. May consent.
A minor whom state law lets consent because they understand the risks. Varies by state.
Federal law, enforced by the DEA, that sorts drugs into Schedules I–V and requires strict tracking.
Taking a client’s controlled drug for personal use or sale. A crime that must be reported.
Protect volunteers who give emergency help outside a job, within their training, without abandoning the victim.
Leaving a person after starting care, before someone qualified takes over.
An employee reporting an employer’s unsafe or illegal practices. The whistleblower is protected from retaliation if conditions are met.
Someone the law requires to report suspected abuse or neglect, on suspicion, without proof.

sections.heading: What makes consent “informed”?
sections.keyIdea: The provider explains and gets consent. The nurse confirms understanding, arranges an interpreter, and witnesses.
sections.body:
Consent is valid only when the client has capacity, gets enough information, and chooses freely. It is needed for surgery, diagnostic procedures, and sedation. It is not needed for urgent, lifesaving emergency care.

The provider doing the procedure explains it. The nurse checks that the client can see, hear, and read. The nurse uses a qualified medical interpreter, never family, and respects cultural and spiritual needs.

Witnessing confirms the signer is the client, the choice is free, and the client seems to understand. If the client is unsure, don’t witness; call the provider back. Consent can be withdrawn anytime. If it is, stop, notify the provider, and document. Get it before giving opioids or sedatives.
bullets: Reason: why treatment is needed.
Procedure: what will be done.
Benefits: how it helps and what to expect.
Risks: possible bad outcomes.
Alternatives: other options, including no treatment.

table.caption: Types of consent
rows: “Yes, draw my blood,” or a signed form
Holding out an arm for a BP
Signed after talking with the surgeon

check.q: Before signing, a client says, “The surgeon talked so fast. I’m not sure what they’re taking out.” What should the nurse do?
check.a: Don’t witness yet. Notify the surgeon, who must explain before consent is valid.

sections.heading: What if the client can’t decide?
sections.keyIdea: Presume adults can decide. If capacity is in doubt, tell the provider. If it is lost, use the guardian, surrogate, or directive.
sections.body:
The emergency doctrine never allows a treatment the client already refused. If a Jehovah’s Witness refused blood, maybe on a wallet card, giving blood after they pass out is battery. Use accepted alternatives and involve ethics as needed.

Competency is legal. If a court finds an adult incompetent, it appoints a guardian. Capacity is clinical and can be lost for a while from opioids, sedation, illness, or delirium, or slowly from dementia. A diagnosis alone doesn’t remove the right to decide.

Under the Patient Self-Determination Act, Medicare and Medicaid hospitals must ask about advance directives. Directives reduce family conflict.
steps: Presume the adult can decide.
Watch for confusion, sedation, or trouble repeating information.
Tell the provider before consent is signed.
For a guardian, confirm the court order is on the chart.
If capacity is lost with no guardian, find the surrogate per directive, law, and policy.
sections.example: A client with early Alzheimer disease can explain why she needs cataract surgery, what will happen, and that glasses are the alternative. She has capacity for this decision. Her daughter’s preference doesn’t override her.

check.q: An unconscious, bleeding crash victim has a signed card refusing blood. What applies?
check.a: The emergency doctrine doesn’t override a known refusal. Tell the provider; don’t give blood; use alternatives.

sections.heading: When can a minor consent?
sections.keyIdea: A parent usually consents for anyone under 18, but several legal exceptions let the minor decide.
sections.body: A parent or guardian usually consents for a minor (under 18). When a law lets the minor consent to a service, the minor is the decision maker for it. Elective surgery for a non-emancipated minor needs a parent.
bullets: An emergency.
Emancipation: independent of parents, such as married or in the military.
Mature-minor law, in some states for some 14- and 15-year-olds.
A court order.
A law for a specific service: a minor parent for their own child, or contraception, prenatal, STI, mental health, or substance care.

table.caption: Box 49.2 — Minor consent across states (CDC/Guttmacher data)
rows: 27 states + DC allow all minors (from 12 or 14); 19 allow some groups; 4 have no specific law
45 states + DC allow all minors 12+; HI, NH, ND, ID from 14; SC from 16
33 states + DC; 14 of these let providers inform parents
28 states + DC let minor parents place a child
30 states + DC let minor parents consent
2 states + DC allow all minors; 21 require a parent’s consent; 10 require notice

sections.example: Clinical Example A: Marvin, 15, has relapsed leukemia. He accepts a bone marrow transplant but refuses resuscitation. His parents want everything. The nurse knows the state’s mature-minor law and policy and helps Marvin, his parents, the team, and the ethics committee talk. The nurse supports Marvin’s voice but doesn’t settle the conflict alone.

check.q: A 16-year-old mother brings her baby for shots. Who consents?
check.a: Where state law allows, she does. The grandparent doesn’t, unless a legal guardian.

sections.heading: Controlled drugs: what does the law require?
sections.keyIdea: The CSA sorts drugs into Schedules I–V. Nurses secure, count, waste with a watching witness, and report gaps.
sections.body:
The CSA is federal law enforced by the DEA. It sorts drugs by medical use and abuse risk and tracks them from maker to client. Store controlled drugs securely and count them per policy. Waste with a licensed witness who actually watches. Report any count gap right away. Having a controlled drug without a prescription is a crime.

Diversion is a crime. Report concerns factually through the chain of command and to the Board as required. Don’t confront or investigate alone.
bullets: Diversion cue: frequent wastes with no witness.
Diversion cue: clients whose pain stays uncontrolled after large doses.
Diversion cue: offering to give others’ opioids, frequent breaks, behavior changes.

check.q: A busy coworker offers to cosign a morphine waste later. What should the nurse do?
check.a: Decline. The witness must watch the waste.

sections.heading: Good Samaritan laws and whistleblowing
sections.keyIdea: Good Samaritan law protects unpaid help within your training. Whistleblower law protects reporting a real violation, inside first.
sections.body:
Good Samaritan laws protect you when you volunteer in an emergency outside a job. Stay within your training; don’t try a field tracheostomy. Stay until EMS or someone qualified takes over. Paid care, gross negligence, and willful misconduct are not covered.

A whistleblower reports an employer’s unsafe or illegal practices. The 1989 Whistleblower Protection Act covers federal employees. Most nurses are protected by OSHA provisions and state laws. Use internal channels first, unless already threatened or punished. The report must involve a specific law or rule, not a simple error. Retaliation is not allowed.

Whistleblower steps:
steps: Document the problem factually.
Report through the chain of command.
Give written notice and time to fix it.
If not fixed, report to the right agency.
If retaliated against, file with OSHA promptly, before resigning.

check.q: An off-duty nurse starts CPR, then leaves before EMS arrives. Protected?
check.a: Possibly not. Leaving before qualified help takes over is abandonment.

rows: Inside first; written notice; a specific law
Skips inside channels; simple error; resigns before filing

sections.heading: Reporting abuse and keeping teen confidences
sections.keyIdea: Report reasonable suspicion of abuse without proof. Tell teens privacy has limits.
sections.body:
Nurses must report suspected child abuse and neglect, per policy and personally to the proper agency. You need suspicion, not proof; proof is the investigators’ job. Report in good faith. The reporter’s name is generally kept private. Failing to report can bring civil, and in many states criminal, penalties.

Any bruise on a non-mobile infant suggests abuse. Vomiting and lethargy may mean head injury. In older children, watch for injuries that don’t fit the story. Sexual abuse often leaves no physical signs.

For vulnerable adults, signs include untreated pressure injuries, soiled bedding, and no food. Report to adult protective services. Then meet the client’s needs, document, and notify the provider. Teaching the caregiver doesn’t replace the report.

Teens deserve honest privacy. Explain the limits: danger, abuse, and insurance statements sent to a parent. Never promise total secrecy.

When you suspect child abuse:
steps: Spot injuries that don’t fit the story or development.
Make the child safe and treat injuries.
Document facts and exact words.
Report promptly; don’t wait for proof.
Don’t confront or investigate.

check.q: A 15-year-old asks, “Promise you won’t tell my mom?” Best response?
check.a: “Most things stay private, but if someone is in danger, I have to share it.”

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: The nurse witnesses but doesn’t explain, emergencies don’t override refusals, and abuse needs suspicion, not proof.
sections.body: Sort these pairs out before test day.

rows: The provider explains; the nurse witnesses.
Independent of parents vs. state recognizes understanding.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Ask: did the client truly understand, from the person doing it, without pressure? If not, fix that gap.
sections.body:
Sample: A client who speaks Vietnamese needs a cardiac catheterization. The adult son offers to translate. What should the nurse do?
A. Let the son interpret.
B. Get a qualified medical interpreter.
C. Have the client nod, then witness.
D. Give a translated form and witness.
steps: Read the stem: a language barrier, a relative offering to help, and an invasive procedure.
What is it really asking? The nurse’s role in valid consent.
Key cue: “son offers to translate.” Family may soften or filter information.
Why A is wrong: being fluent doesn’t make him a medical interpreter.
Why C is wrong: a nod isn’t informed consent.
Why D is wrong: a form doesn’t replace the provider’s talk and questions.
The answer is B. The provider explains through the interpreter; then the nurse witnesses.
Strategy: pick the action that closes the understanding gap: interpreter, call the provider, or delay sedation.

sections.heading: Worked case: the bruised infant
sections.keyIdea: Treat the possible head injury first, then report the suspicion yourself.
sections.body: A 4-month-old is lethargic and vomiting, with fingertip bruises on both arms. The boyfriend says she rolled off the couch, but she can’t roll yet. The provider says, “We’ll sort out the bruises later.”
steps: Cues: bruises on a non-mobile infant, signs of head injury, and a story that doesn’t fit.
Physical safety first: arrange ED transport and watch airway, breathing, and neuro status.
Know your duty: suspicion is enough. The provider’s “later” doesn’t remove the nurse’s own duty.
Report promptly to the child protective agency (in NC, the county DSS).
Don’t promise the boyfriend secrecy, and don’t accuse him.
Document the bruise pattern on a body diagram, his exact words, and the report made.
Include the safety concern in the ED handoff.

check.q: The boyfriend asks who reported. What should the nurse say?
check.a: Don’t reveal it. The reporter’s identity is generally kept confidential. Focus on the baby’s safety and care.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: NC is a universal reporting state: anyone who suspects child maltreatment must report to the county DSS.
sections.body: These NC laws guide practice here.
bullets: G.S. 7B-301: any person or institution that suspects a juvenile (under 18) is abused, neglected, or dependent, or died from maltreatment, reports to the county DSS director.
Knowingly failing to report is a crime in NC. Report suspicion; don’t investigate or wait for proof. Good-faith reporters are immune.
G.S. 108A-102: anyone with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult needs protective services reports to the county DSS director, orally or in writing. Good-faith reporters are immune.

G.S. 90-21.5: minors may consent for STIs and other reportable diseases, pregnancy (not sterilization or abortion), substance or alcohol abuse, and emotional disturbance. Emancipated minors may consent. Majority is 18.
G.S. 90-21.14: Good Samaritan protection for unpaid emergency care, unless gross negligence, wanton conduct, or intentional wrongdoing. Not for paid work.
Advance directives: Health Care Power of Attorney (G.S. Chapter 32A, Article 3) and living will (G.S. 90-321). The portable order form is the MOST (Medical Orders for Scope of Treatment).
Diversion is reported to the NCBON, which offers alternative-to-discipline programs for substance use.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body: Source: Module 49 study guide, pp. 2831–2834.
bullets: Pp. 2831–2832: consent, capacity, competency, emergency doctrine. Pp. 2832–2833: minors, Box 49.2, Clinical Example A, CSA, Table 49.2, Good Samaritan, whistleblowing. P. 2834: lifespan and traps.
The CSA is enforced by the Drug Enforcement Administration (the course says “Agency”).
Table 49.2 calls Schedule V “no Rx required.” Many, like pregabalin, need a prescription; only some low-dose codeine products may be sold under pharmacist control where state law allows.
Ezogabine, the course’s Schedule V example, was discontinued in 2017, so pregabalin is used.
Federal rescheduling of marijuana to Schedule III has been under review since 2024; check its status. The NCLEX tests schedule concepts.
The course says failing to report child abuse may bring civil charges. Many states, including NC, make it a crime.
The 1989 Act covers federal employees; other nurses rely on OSHA provisions and state laws, which have deadlines.
Adult protective services reporting, the Patient Self-Determination Act, consent before sedation, and waste practice were added as standard practice.

mnemonics.name: RPBRA — the five consent elements
mnemonics.text: Reason, Procedure, Benefits, Risks, Alternatives (including no treatment). “Real Patients Bravely Review Alternatives.”

mnemonics.name: Good Samaritan = “Free, Fit, Finish”
mnemonics.text: Free: no pay, not on duty. Fit: within your training. Finish: stay until qualified help takes over.

pearls: The provider obtains consent; the nurse witnesses.
Never use family to interpret consent.
Confirm a guardian’s court order on the chart.
Dementia or mental illness alone doesn’t remove the right to consent.
Tell teens privacy is kept when possible, not guaranteed.
redFlags: Consent signed while sedated or confused.
A controlled-drug count gap or an unwitnessed waste.
An off-duty nurse leaving an emergency victim before qualified help takes over.

checks.q: A client got hydromorphone 30 minutes ago and is drowsy when the surgeon brings the consent for a nonemergency procedure. What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Tell the surgeon about the recent opioid and drowsiness. Delay consent until the client has capacity, because consent signed while sedated may not be valid.

checks.q: A 17-year-old who is married and lives on her own needs an appendectomy. Who signs?
checks.a: She does. She is an emancipated minor; marriage and living independently are typical emancipation criteria.

checks.q: A client with schizophrenia, not under guardianship, clearly explains why he refuses elective hernia surgery. Can the team go ahead on the psychiatrist’s word?
checks.a: No. Mental illness alone doesn’t remove the right to refuse, and he shows capacity for this decision. Going ahead would be battery. Document and notify the provider.

checks.q: On a home visit, an older adult with dementia lies in soiled bedding with a new pressure injury and no food in the house. The caregiver says, “She refuses help.” What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Report suspected neglect to adult protective services (in NC, the county DSS director). Reasonable cause is enough. Meet her needs, document facts and the caregiver’s words, and notify the provider. Don’t threaten or investigate.

checks.q: A 14-year-old asks for STI testing and wants her parents not told. How should the nurse respond in most states?
checks.a: Most states let minors consent to STI care. Give care confidentially within the law, and honestly explain the limits, such as insurance statements and safety concerns.

checks.q: An off-duty nurse at a restaurant helps a choking man and is later sued. What decides whether she is protected?
checks.a: Whether she helped without pay, stayed within her training, avoided gross negligence or willful misconduct, and stayed until qualified help took over.
